departments.headline: GOBLINS ALL THE WAY DOWN
departments.dek: Why would a deck full of 1/1 Goblins bother with a one-mana spell that just says 'draw a card'? Because with Zada, Hedron Grinder on the battlefield, that spell doesn't say that anymore.

callouts.title: BODIES FIRST
callouts.text: Turns one through three are for Goblins, not for plans. Dragon Fodder, Krenko's Command and Mogg War Marshal are cheap on purpose, and the simulation has your first token maker arriving on turn 3.18 on average. Every body you add is a card the engine will draw later.

callouts.title: LAND THE GRINDER
callouts.text: Zada costs {3}{R} and arrives on turn 4 in 7,002 of 10,000 simulated games. Cast her as a 3/3 and pass. She does nothing the turn she lands, and that is the point — the table has to look somewhere else for one more rotation.

callouts.title: SPEND THE TURN
callouts.text: One red mana into a spell that targets only Zada converts every other creature you control into a card. Verified line 001: four Goblins in, five cards and a hasted team out. That is the floor of this deck, not the ceiling.

captions.Zada, Hedron Grinder: **THE MULTIPLIER:** she does nothing by herself. She changes what every other card in the deck says.
captions.Dragon Fodder: **THE FUEL:** two 1/1s for two mana is two extra cards three turns from now. Bodies aren't an army here — they're the multiplier.
captions.Krenko, Mob Boss: **THE BURST:** five Goblins from one tap, and — verified line 004 — exactly one tap. He is a payoff, not a loop.

pilot_tips.text: Play him on turn one as a Goblin, not as a mana plan — he is a body first and a ritual second.
Never fire a cantrip at Zada for two copies of value; wait until at least three other creatures are on the battlefield.

departments.pull_quote: A board that reads as chump blockers until the turn it draws five cards and kills the table.

departments.headline: THE CHEAPEST ENGINE IN THE ZONE
departments.dek: Your commander is the one card you are guaranteed to have — so what is that worth when the card is a 3/3 that does nothing on its own? More than you think, and it stops being cheap faster than you think.
departments.body:
Start with the rule that makes Commander a different game. CR 903.6: "At the start of the game, each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone." Zada, Hedron Grinder is not a card you hope to draw. She is a card you already have, face up, before the first mulligan is even offered — and in this deck she is a specific physical object, the borderless foil Secret Lair printing, collector number 2406, the first card of a thirteen-card drop that Featured Artist takes apart later in the issue. It is the only card in the game you get to point at before anyone has drawn anything. That single fact inverts opening-hand logic, and it is why the keep rule in Keep or Ship asks you for lands and bodies and never once asks you for a payoff. The payoff is already on the table.

Now the bill. The ladder beside this file is CR 903.8: a commander cast from the command zone "costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." For Zada that reads four mana, then six, then eight. Put those numbers next to your own: the simulation gives you 3.94 mean available mana on turn 4, 5.18 on turn 6, and still only 6.96 on turn 10. The first cast is on curve. The second — six mana — is realistically a turn-8 play in a deck whose land-drop rate has already fallen to 41% by then. The third is not a turn; it is a ritual.

So which do you buy: insurance or speed? The strategy companion prices it honestly — protection slots and held mana cost you every game, while removal only costs you some. This deck's entire engine routes through one creature, which argues hard for constant protection. But Swiftfoot Boots cast before Zada is two mana that made no Goblins, and decision spread 001 shows exactly what that costs: pushing Zada to turn 5 pushes the engine to turn 6 or 7, past the window where a sweeper deck has held up mana twice. Our rule: the Boots go down after the table has proven Zada must die, not before. Against a pod that has already spent its removal, pay the tax once and rebuild. Against a pod holding everything, protect on the pivot turn and only then.

Color identity is the other bill, and it is bigger. CR 903.4 governs the 99 by the mana symbols in your commander's cost and rules text, and Zada's identity is a single red pip. You therefore do not get the blue one-target cantrips that make Zada a genuine combo deck in other shells, you do not get a counterspell to protect the engine turn, and you do not get efficient white removal. Your entire interaction suite is Chaos Warp, Vandalblast, Gempalm Incinerator, Goblin Trashmaster and Blasphemous Act — five cards, and you should know all five by name. What mono-red buys back: twenty-two Mountains that cast literally everything, a Ruby Medallion that discounts every nonland card in the deck except the artifacts, and rituals like Brightstone Ritual and Battle Hymn that scale off Goblins instead of lands. That last one matters more than it looks, because your land-drop rate is falling all game and your Goblin count is not.

Is the 21-damage clock real here? No — but the arithmetic is closer than you would guess, so know it. CR 903.10a: "A player who's been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game." Zada is a 3/3, which is seven connections, and this deck never wants to attack with her seven times. But verified line 003 has her swinging as a 10/3 with trample off a single Fists of Flame, and two turns like that is 20. Track the number on one opponent as a tiebreaker; never build toward it. This deck's real reach is each-opponent damage — Impact Tremors, Grapeshot, and a wide hasted alpha strike — because incremental combat damage does not cross three opponents and roughly 120 combined life.

Finally, the political read. When Zada resolves, anyone who has seen this deck once starts counting your untapped Mountains; she is your loudest tell, and the simulation has her on the battlefield by turn 6 in 90% of games. The good news is that she is a 3/3 doing nothing on arrival, and threat deflection is cheapest when the board agrees with you. Cast her into a table that is staring at somebody else's board, pass, and let the pod spend its answers on the player who is visibly winning. The turn you point one red mana at her is the turn you become the archenemy — so make sure it is also the turn they have to answer you or start dying.

captions.Zada, Hedron Grinder: **THE COMMANDER FILE:** {3}{R}, mono-red, on the battlefield by turn 6 in 90% of 10,000 simulated games — and four mana the first time, six the second, eight the third.
captions.Mountain: **WHAT MONO-RED BUYS BACK:** twenty-two of them, and every single one casts every card in the deck. That is the compensation for the counterspell you are never going to get to hold.

pilot_tips.text: Hold these until the table has proven Zada has to die — protection bought before anyone shows removal is two mana that made no Goblins.
Play it the turn you draw it: 716 of 10,000 simulated games put Zada on the battlefield by turn 2, and fast mana is the only thing that gets you there.

departments.pull_quote: Four mana, then six, then eight. The command zone is a guarantee, not a subscription.

departments.headline: TEN THOUSAND GOLDFISH
departments.dek: How often does this deck actually do the thing? We ran the list 10,000 times on seed 42 — and one of these numbers is here specifically to disappoint you.

callouts.title: 79.1% KEEPABLE
callouts.text: 79.1% of first sevens are keeps, and the deck averages 0.26 mulligans. That is what a curve made almost entirely of ones and twos buys you: you are rarely the player starting on six.

callouts.title: TURN 4, SEVENTY PERCENT OF THE TIME
callouts.text: The commander cast-turn histogram spikes hard — 7,002 of 10,000 games cast Zada on turn 4 exactly. Mean 4.35, median 4, 90% by turn 6. Your engine window is not a vibe; it is a date.

callouts.title: THE NUMBER THAT SAYS NO
callouts.text: 'Storm payoff plus ritual drawn' assembles in 15.2% of games, and only 9.1% by turn 6. The storm kill is this deck's ceiling, not its plan. Read every other page with that number in your pocket.

pilot_tips.text: Get it down before the engine turn, not after — a five-draw Zada turn puts you well over seven cards and cleanup takes the difference.
Don't build a turn around it. Cast it as a token maker at a small storm count and be happy — the simulation only draws a payoff-plus-ritual pair in 15.2% of games.

departments.pull_quote: The storm kill is the ceiling. The Zada draw engine is the floor — and the floor is where you live.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and the renderer prints all assumptions verbatim. Never let a meter caption read as a prediction: these runs model resource development, not games.

departments.headline: THE TURN IT ALL PAYS
departments.dek: Five lines went to the adversarial checker and all five came back clean. Four of them are ways to win the game; the fifth is a famous combo this deck does not have — and that one is the reason you should believe the other four.

callouts.title: ONE RED MANA
callouts.text: Cast Crimson Wisps targeting only Zada, Hedron Grinder. Only her. The 'targets only' clause is the entire engine and it is trivially easy to break by adding a second target out of habit.

callouts.title: THE TRIGGER GOES ON TOP
callouts.text: Zada's ability triggers on the cast and sits above the spell, so it resolves first. It copies the spell for each other creature you control that the spell could target — four Goblin tokens, four copies, each aimed at a different one, in the order you choose.

callouts.title: COUNT YOUR CASTS, NOT YOUR RESOLUTIONS
callouts.text: The copies are put on the stack, not cast. Zada does not re-trigger off her own copies, and none of them raise the storm count for a later Grapeshot. This is the single most common way a pilot miscounts a storm turn; the rule number is in the dossier.

callouts.title: FIVE CARDS FOR {R}
callouts.text: Four copies and then the original resolve. Every creature you control is red with haste and you have drawn five cards for one mana. Full dossier: Judge's Desk, Case A-001.

captions.Haze of Rage: **THE REAL ONE:** buyback returns the card, storm multiplies it, and Storm-Kiln pays for the next cast. Verified line 005.
captions.Storm-Kiln Artist: **THE PAYMASTER:** a Treasure for every cast and every copy — which is why the loop funds itself from cast three onward.
captions.Fists of Flame: **THE FINISHER:** each copy draws before it buffs, so the later copies lock in the biggest numbers. 32 power of trample.

pilot_tips.text: Never sacrifice Krenko to Skirk Prospector expecting him back — we checked, and in this deck he does not come back.
Don't start the loop until three real spells have already been cast this turn; that is the cast count that makes each buyback pay for itself.
Deploy the Artist last. The moment it is on the battlefield with four mana up, an informed table has to treat you as lethal.
Every card you drew earlier this turn makes every copy bigger — cast your other cantrips first, and let the original resolve last on your biggest body.

departments.pull_quote: The database said infinite. The rules said no.
departments.note: This is the peak spread and gets the most ambitious layout in the issue. Line 004 must be given equal feature weight to the four winning lines — it is the best story in the issue.

departments.headline: WHEN THEY DECIDE IT'S YOU
departments.dek: Nobody kills the Goblin player for having Goblins. So what exactly are three opponents looking at on the turn they all turn around at once?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW A
callouts.text: Zada untapped, three or more other creatures, one red mana open. Verified line 001 says that board is five cards for {R}, and any opponent who has seen this deck once knows it. This is the window you are hiding until you can use.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW B
callouts.text: Storm-Kiln Artist on the battlefield, four mana up, Haze of Rage in hand. Verified line 005 makes that a mana-positive loop that strictly improves every iteration. Treat the first Haze cast as your commitment point and fire it when the table's interaction is tapped or spent, not when it is convenient.

callouts.title: THE FALSE ALARM
callouts.text: Krenko, Mob Boss resolving looks exactly like the Spellbook infinite and is not it. When an opponent panic-removes him, they have paid a real card for a one-shot payoff. Sometimes the correct play is to let them.

captions.Conspicuous Snoop: **THE TELL:** the Snoop shows your library top to the whole table, all game. Deploy it when you want to look busy.
captions.Skullclamp: **THE OTHER TELL:** a clamp on an empty-ish board still screams engine deck. The table reads it before you use it.

pilot_tips.text: You can only goad a creature controlled by the player you just damaged — so choose who you attack by whose blockers you want pointed somewhere else.
The Snoop shows your library's top card to the whole table all game; deploy it when you want to look busy, not on the turn you are quietly setting up.

departments.pull_quote: You are not hiding. You are being boring on purpose, for exactly as long as it takes.

departments.headline: TWO TURNS, NO HINTS
departments.dek: Cover the verdict box with your hand before you read the branches. One of these is turn three with your commander still in hand; the other is turn six with a wrath telegraphed across the table.

callouts.title: HOW TO PLAY ALONG
callouts.text: Read the board, commit to a branch out loud, then read ours. Being wrong on this page is free. Being wrong on turn six is a game.

pilot_tips.text: Never hold it to 'stay open' — it adds red for each Goblin on the battlefield, so it scales with the exact board you would be declining to build.
Against a telegraphed sweeper, keep this one in hand. Two Goblins after the wrath are worth more than two Goblins in front of it.

departments.pull_quote: The engine's draw count is set by bodies on the battlefield at resolution time. Hiding costs cards.
departments.note: The recommendation must stay visually below the branches — the reader commits first, we answer second.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: Three of these four archetypes you are fine against, and one of them takes your deck apart piece by piece. Can you name it before you read the meters?

threats.read: Their board is four open mana and a patient expression, and over a four-player game the wrath is close to certain — so the question is never whether to play into it, only what you bank first. Your engine is the insurance, not the victim: verified line 001 turns four bodies into five cards in a zone no sweeper touches, and Storm-Kiln Artist's Treasures ride straight through a creature wrath. When the sweeper is telegraphed at sorcery speed, fire the cantrip engine now and bank the draws.

This is the one. Taxes attack your velocity math directly — a two-spell turn becoming a one-spell turn halves the engine, and you should physically recount your hand under every new tax. One lock piece is an inconvenience; the second and third are the lock. You do not own the long game here, so you are the beatdown and you are racing their assembly. Name your outs before you need them and sequence to protect the one that breaks the piece that actually beats you, not the scariest permanent on the table.

You win these on asymmetry rather than size. Gempalm Incinerator cycles to deal damage equal to the number of Goblins on the battlefield — theirs count too — and Blasphemous Act gets cheaper for every creature in play, which in a token mirror means their board pays for your reset. Let the other wide deck be the archenemy and out-grind it: Impact Tremors and a hasted alpha strike drain every opponent without ever attacking into a blocker.

Your interaction is three cards deep, so held answers rot: rank their combo proximity above every board threat and plan to disrupt once, cheaply, at the decisive moment rather than saving an answer for a better one. Your own race line is real but narrow — the simulation assembles a storm payoff with a ritual in 15.2% of games — so do not plan to out-speed a dedicated combo deck. Apply pressure so their tapped-out setup turn is punished, and let Grenzo goads pull their blockers apart.

captions.Blasphemous Act: **THE RESET:** cheaper for every creature on the table, so a token mirror pays for your wrath and not theirs.
captions.Vandalblast: **THE UNLOCK:** overload it on the piece that beats you, not on the most artifacts.

pilot_tips.text: Overload it when it breaks the specific piece that beats you, not when it kills the most artifacts — those are usually different turns.
Count every creature on the table, not just yours, before you assume it costs nine — in a token mirror it is frequently a two-mana reset you can rebuild from and they cannot.

departments.pull_quote: One lock piece is an inconvenience. The second and third are the lock.

departments.headline: WHY EACH GOBLIN EARNED ITS SLOT
departments.dek: Ninety-nine cards doing four jobs: make bodies, make mana, copy a spell, or end the game. If a card in here does none of those it is on notice — and Upgrade Watch names the one that is.
departments.note: Load-bearing cards lead; everything else is depth and should read as depth. Tiles here are role-first and deliberately do not carry printing credits — the physical cards are Featured Artist's subject two pages later, and splitting that job across both departments would blunt both.

departments.headline: THE DROP THAT LANDED ON THE ENGINE
departments.dek: One artist painted your commander, your mana, your draw engine and your storm kill — and not one of the eight spells Zada actually reads. Is that taste, or is it a receipt?

featured.note:
Fourteen of the eighty cards counted here are Wizard of Barge's — the drop's two table-aid cards are his too, but they have no rules text, so they do not count — and thirteen of the fourteen arrived in the same box: collector numbers 2406 through 2418, unbroken.

That is a Secret Lair drop bought whole, not a collection assembled card by card, and we are saying so plainly because the coincidence underneath it is a far better story than the flattery would have been. The drop is a Goblin drop; this deck's hardware is Goblin hardware; so one purchase happened to land on the commander, the token engine, the mana base, the draw outlet and the storm kill simultaneously.

What it did not land on is the ammunition. The eight one-target cantrips that turn Zada from a 3/3 into a draw engine — the cards this entire magazine is about — are eight cards by eight different artists, every one of them pulled out of The List one at a time by somebody who knew what the deck needed. Read the roster table below in that light: where the concentration is, a box did the work, and where the dispersion is, a pilot did.

also_worth_noting.note: The only artist here besides the drop with more than three cards, and every one of them arrived separately. Goblin Matron, Mogg War Marshal, a Quest and a Reliquary Tower have nothing in common except him.
Three cards doing three unrelated jobs — a removal spell, a goad engine, and the Boots the Command Zone tells you not to cast early.

Both of the deck's big rituals are hers: Mana Geyser and Seething Song, two Commander 2021 cards that came through The List within three collector numbers of each other. A coincidence, and a pretty one.

captions.Crimson Wisps: **THE AMMUNITION:** Jim Nelson painted this one, and seven other artists painted the other seven spells Zada reads. Eight cards, eight hands, zero overlap with the box.
captions.Grapeshot: **THE KILL, PRE-PACKAGED:** Grapeshot and Empty the Warrens shipped in the same drop as your commander. The storm half of this deck arrived assembled.
captions.Moggcatcher: **THE OUTLIER:** collector number 7081, well outside the #2406–#2418 run. The one Wizard of Barge card in this deck that turned up on its own.

pilot_tips.text: Put the drop's storm counter card on the table before you cast the first spell of a big turn, not three casts in — Case A-002 turns on knowing your count exactly, and nobody has ever reconstructed a storm turn correctly from memory.
Expect the borderless foil to get picked up and read — a table that stops to admire your commander is a table that has now learned what one red mana does, so plan the pivot turn assuming they know.

departments.pull_quote: Thirteen cards in one box — and not one of them is a cantrip Zada reads.
departments.note: Hero is the commander's art_crop. Every number on this spread is computed by `manamap pilot artist-credits` and recomputed at render time — the plan supplies the choice and the argument, never the counts. The honesty notes stay under the gallery, unabridged. The argument is the hardware/ammunition split; do not let the gallery drift into a receipt with compliments attached.

departments.headline: FOUR SEVENS, FOUR VERDICTS
departments.dek: 79.1% of your first sevens are keeps, which makes the interesting question not whether to keep but which of these four you would ship anyway. Decide on each one before you read the reason.

hands.why: Three lands, a one-mana body, a two-mana token maker, and the cantrip banked for the turn after Zada lands. Your commander is already in the command zone at {3}{R}, so this hand does not need a payoff — it needs mana and Goblins, and it has both.

hands.verdict: KEEP — two lands and fast mana
hands.why: Sol Ring on turn one is how 716 of 10,000 simulated games get Zada down on turn 2. Two token makers keep the curve honest and Faithless Looting turns the stranded Blasphemous Act into live cards.

Every card here is the back half of a turn you have no way to start. Rituals and storm payoffs do nothing without a board and a spell count, and 'storm payoff plus ritual drawn' assembles in only 15.2% of games. This hand is not the 15.2% — it is the hand that makes people think they are in it.

hands.verdict: SHIP — six lands and a tutor
hands.why: Goblin Matron finds you exactly one Goblin on turn three and then you are drawing off the top with a curve that mostly stops at three. Surplus lands are not a resource in this deck — they are blanks with a cycling cost attached.

captions.Faithless Looting: **THE UPGRADE:** turns a marginal keep into a live one. It has never once been a land.

pilot_tips.text: Count it as half a card when you are deciding a marginal keep — it upgrades dead cards into live ones, but it has never once been a land.
Three bodies on one card makes him the best two-drop in a borderline keep — just plan for the echo, and be happy to let him die into his second token.

departments.pull_quote: Your opening hand does not need a payoff. The payoff is face up in the command zone before you look at your seven.

departments.headline: THE MACHINE'S SHOPPING LIST, AUDITED
departments.dek: The obsolescence index does not know this is a Goblin deck, and it has never read the words 'targets only Zada.' Here is what it got right, what it got funny, and what you should quietly ignore.

pilot_tips.text: The index says Grapeshot obsoletes it — and you already run Grapeshot, so cut Insurrection first the moment you find something you like better.
Ignore the index here: its damage scales with every Goblin on the battlefield, and no 'strictly better' card in the index can see a creature type.
It is already sitting in your sideboard — try it in the Witch's Mark slot for a few games and see which one you actually miss.

departments.pull_quote: The index compares functions. It cannot see a creature type, and it has never read the words 'targets only Zada.'
departments.note: Parroting the index unaudited is the one thing this department is not allowed to do.

departments.headline: FIVE CASE FILES, ONE REVISION
departments.dek: Every citation, verbatim, in the order the rules actually apply. Case A-003 needed two passes — the checker caught a missing state-based-action step and sent the resolution back, which is precisely what it is for.
departments.note: Renderer-generated from the checker-passed artifacts. Nothing here may be summarized, truncated or paraphrased.

rhythm_notes: The canonical order already alternates correctly for this deck: By the Numbers (analysis, dense) is followed by The Kill (narrative), and Know Your Enemy (reference, dense) is followed by The 99 (browsing). The two places that needed deliberate work were the approach to the peak and the descent from it. Approaching: First Turns opens with a question and three callout steps rather than prose, so the reader arrives at The Command Zone already curious rather than already tired, and By the Numbers gets a pull quote as its exit ramp so the reader leaves a dense data spread on a sentence instead of a table. Descending: The Kill is the peak and carries the heaviest furniture in the issue, so The Politics Table deliberately runs on reflection and callouts only, no new mechanics, as the breather. What's Your Play? then spikes back up on participation before Know Your Enemy settles into reference. The 99 is the browsing valley by design; Upgrade Watch and Judge's Desk are opt-in depth. The 99 and Featured Artist now form a two-department valley — browsing into appreciation, both low intensity — the longest exhale in the issue, sitting exactly where a reader who has just been quizzed and drilled on matchups needs it. Featured Artist also carries the issue's second honest-negative beat: The Kill refuses to call a famous combo infinite, and Featured Artist refuses to call a bulk purchase a curatorial statement. Putting those at opposite ends of the recovery arc asserts our credibility twice without either reading as an apology.
gaps: Two candidate lines from strategic_frame.json are still unresolved and both would be strong Kill features. Roaming Throne naming Goblin, doubling Zada's copy trigger, is the more valuable one: the card is in the 99, the interaction is genuinely non-obvious, and nobody at the table knows the answer. Past in Flames rebuilding a ritual chain for a second Grapeshot is the second.

Only two decision spreads exist. The obvious third is the Haze of Rage commitment turn — Storm-Kiln Artist down, four mana up, one opponent with counterspell mana — which would close the loop between the issue's headline verified infinite and the department that makes the reader decide.

cards.json has no art_crop or artist fields, so hero art renders card scans rather than the borderless full-art crops with artist credit that STYLEv3 §9 sets as the target standard. Blocked on printing metadata in the deck ingestion step.
Strategy DB gaps this issue routed around: no commander-damage / clock section to ground the 21-damage answer in The Command Zone.

Data question for the goldfish artifact: keep_first_seven_rate is 0.791, but the published land_histogram puts 9,899 of 10,000 first sevens at 2-5 lands under the stated keep rule. The issue cites 79.1% verbatim and never derives it, but the two figures cannot both be describing the same test — the artifact should document what else the keep rule checks, or the histogram should state which population it counts.

artist-credits computes a per-set breakdown the renderer does not surface: 63 of 80 counted cards came through The List across 53 artists, against 17 from Secret Lair across 4. That dispersion is the second-best art story in the deck and is currently only reachable through authored prose. Worth a row in the Art File.

Three Secret Lair cards — Moggcatcher, Broadside Bombardiers, Roaming Throne — have no role group in The 99 and fall into the unlabeled Depth bucket. They are in the deck because they came in the box, which is a legitimate roster fact the roster neither states nor gives them a job for.
